## The data

The **Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance** table from the US Bureau of Transportation
Statistics ([TranStats](https://www.transtats.bts.gov/)) has one row per domestic flight
operated by large US airlines. It records scheduled and actual times, delays, cancellations,
diversions and their causes. My assigned month was **January 2024**: one CSV of 247 MB,
**547,271 rows** and 110 columns.

## Star schema

The data is organized as a star schema: one fact table of flight events, plus small lookup
(dimension) tables that turn codes into readable names.

```{mermaid}
erDiagram
    al_perf }o--|| L_AIRLINE_ID : "DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline = ID"
    al_perf }o--|| L_AIRPORT : "Origin / Dest = Code"
    al_perf }o--|| L_AIRPORT_ID : "OriginAirportID / DestAirportID = ID"
    al_perf }o--o| L_CANCELATION : "CancellationCode = Code"
    al_perf }o--|| L_WEEKDAYS : "DayOfWeek = Code"
    al_perf }o--|| L_DISTANCE_GROUP_250 : "DistanceGroup = Code"
    al_perf {
        int DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline
        text Origin
        text Dest
        text FlightDate
        int DayOfWeek
        text DepTime
        decimal DepDelay
        double Cancelled
        text CancellationCode
        int DistanceGroup
    }
    L_AIRLINE_ID { int ID text Name }
    L_AIRPORT { text Code text Name }
    L_AIRPORT_ID { int ID text Name }
    L_CANCELATION { text Code text Reason }
    L_WEEKDAYS { int Code text Day }
    L_DISTANCE_GROUP_250 { int Code text DistanceInterval }
```

| Dimension table | Rows | Joins to fact column(s) |
|---|---:|---|
| `L_AIRLINE_ID` | 1,665 | `DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline` |
| `L_AIRPORT` | 6,545 | `Origin`, `Dest` |
| `L_AIRPORT_ID` | 6,527 | `OriginAirportID`, `DestAirportID` |
| `L_CANCELATION` | 4 | `CancellationCode` |
| `L_DISTANCE_GROUP_250` | 11 | `DistanceGroup` |
| `L_WEEKDAYS` | 8 | `DayOfWeek` |

Every flight's airline, origin airport and day of week found a match in its lookup table,
so inner joins drop no flights.

## Loading pipeline on AWS

The fact table is too large for MySQL Workbench's import wizard, so it was loaded from a
cloud machine with MySQL's bulk loader:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["BTS TranStats<br>zip download"] --> B["Laptop<br>al_perf.csv"]
    B -->|scp| C["AWS EC2<br>Amazon Linux"]
    C -->|mysqlimport| D[("AWS RDS<br>MySQL 8, schema FAA")]
    E["Canvas<br>6 dimension CSVs"] -->|Workbench import wizard| D
    D -->|SQL queries| F["Result CSVs"]
    F --> G["Quarto website<br>Python + Plotly"]
```

1. Created schema `FAA` (UTF-8) and the fact table `al_perf` with the course's `CreateFactTable.sql`.
2. Copied `al_perf.csv` to an EC2 instance with `scp`, installed the MySQL/MariaDB client, and
   ran the bulk load against the RDS endpoint. It loaded **547,271 records**, the CSV's row count minus its header:

   ```bash
   mysqlimport --local --compress --user=admin -p --host=<rds-endpoint> \
     --fields-terminated-by=',' --fields-optionally-enclosed-by='"' \
     --ignore-lines=1 FAA al_perf.csv
   ```
3. Loaded the six dimension tables with Workbench's Table Data Import Wizard.
4. Terminated the EC2 instance (and kept the RDS database) to avoid charges.
5. Ran the [7 queries](questions.qmd), exported each result to CSV, and built this site from
   those CSVs with Quarto, pandas and Plotly. The site never connects to the database.

## Data-cleaning decisions {#cleaning}

**Blank numbers become zeros.** In the CSV, a cancelled flight that never left the gate has
empty `DepTime` and `DepDelay` fields. `mysqlimport` stores an empty numeric field as `0` and
raises a warning (that's most of the ~250,000 import warnings). The database therefore says
those 19,784 flights departed "0 minutes late". For every departure-delay calculation I keep
only rows with a recorded departure time, `DepTime <> ''`. Without that filter, airports and
airlines hit hardest by cancellations would look more punctual than they were. (605 cancelled
flights *did* leave the gate before being cancelled. They keep their real recorded delay.)

**Early departures.** Problem 4 says to count early departures as 0 minutes. I use
`GREATEST(DepDelay, 0)`, which equals BTS's own `DepDelayMinutes` column, and apply the same
rule in Problem 5 and in the site's average-delay charts so all averages are comparable.

**The header row.** The course instructions run `mysqlimport` without `--ignore-lines=1`, which
loads the CSV header as one junk row (Year = 0, `FlightDate` = the text 'FlightDate'). I skipped it at load time.
If it had been loaded, `DELETE FROM al_perf WHERE Year = 0;` would remove it.

**What counts as a flight.** BTS sets `Flights = 1` on every row, including cancelled ones, so
flight counts (Problems 3 and 7) use `COUNT(*)` over all scheduled flights.

**Ties.** Problems 5 and 6b use `RANK()`, which keeps ties rather than picking one row arbitrarily.
Problem 5 had no ties. In Problem 6b, 5 airports had two reasons tied for first, giving 301
rows for 296 airports.

## Verification

Every answer was recomputed independently with pandas directly from the raw CSV (not through
MySQL), and the results matched exactly.

## Limitations

- **One month.** January has winter weather and, in 2024, an unusual safety grounding. These
  patterns should not be read as typical for the whole year.
- **Small samples.** Averages for small airports and rare airline–airport pairs rest on very
  few flights. The site reports those counts alongside the averages.
- **Cause vs. coincidence.** The link between carrier cancellations and the 737 MAX 9 grounding
  comes from timing, airline and airport patterns. The dataset has no aircraft-type column,
  so it can't prove which aircraft was cancelled.

## Tools

AWS RDS (MySQL 8) · AWS EC2 · `mysqlimport` · MySQL Workbench · SQL (CTEs, window
functions `RANK()` and `AVG() OVER`) · Python (pandas, Plotly) · Quarto · GitHub Pages
